business_patterns.top_pattern: TX acute hospital volume surge in HMO and POS
business_patterns.what_is_impacting: Commercial Individual acute hospital spend in TX HMO and POS
business_patterns.pattern_details: TX is the clearest broad utilization story in the analysis. Acute hospital spend rose sharply in both HMO and POS because claim volume increased, while paid per admission fell in both products. This points to a utilization and admission-management issue first, not a broad unit-cost escalation.
business_patterns.why_it_matters: This is the single largest cost driver and will not be offset by smaller pricing or coding fixes elsewhere.
business_patterns.recommended_next_step: Start a TX acute inpatient authorization and admission-management workplan for HMO and POS, focused on preventable admits, level-of-care review, and redirecting avoidable cases to lower-cost settings where appropriate.
evidence_summary: TX HMO acute hospital spend increased by $9.8M on 2,373 more claims, while paid per admit fell by about $678.
TX POS acute hospital spend increased by $5.5M on 1,472 more claims, while paid per admit fell by about $495.
These two TX acute hospital product lines account for more than 80% of the identified positive delta in the top operational findings.

business_patterns.top_pattern: Not Mapped buckets are masking real provider and authorization signals
business_patterns.what_is_impacting: Facility and clinical classification across CA, CO, and UNATTRIBUTED
business_patterns.pattern_details: A material share of the increase sits in Not Mapped facility or clinical buckets, so teams cannot reliably tell whether the issue is utilization, provider mix, or classification error. The biggest examples include Orange County Global Medical Center in CA, outpatient drug cases in UNATTRIBUTED, and CORAM CVS Specialty Infusion Services in CO. This is a gating validation pattern: mapping and coding should be corrected before the confirmed claims are reassigned to UM, network, or clinical workflows.
business_patterns.why_it_matters: If unmapped claims are not fixed first, the organization risks chasing false provider or authorization trends.
business_patterns.recommended_next_step: Run a targeted mapping and coding correction pass for Not Mapped facility and outpatient clinical buckets in CA, CO, and UNATTRIBUTED, then reclassify confirmed claims into the proper operational and clinical review queues.
business_patterns.validation_reason: Not Mapped facility and clinical buckets are materially contributing to the increase across multiple segments and providers, so attribution is not reliable enough for direct action without correction.
evidence_summary: CA HMO Not Mapped facility claims at Orange County Global Medical Center added $427K from 1 claim.
UNATTRIBUTED OP Mgmt Oth Misc / Not Mapped / Drugs added $328K from 2 claims.
CO HMO Not Mapped facility claims at CORAM CVS Specialty Infusion Services added $78K from 3 claims.
CA EPO Not Mapped facility claims tied to Stephen L Hofkin added $36K despite 1 fewer claim.

business_patterns.top_pattern: ME, NH, and OH HMO acute spend is concentrated in a few very expensive admissions
business_patterns.what_is_impacting: Commercial Individual HMO acute hospital and IP Med/Surg spend in ME, NH, and OH
business_patterns.pattern_details: This is a low-volume outlier pattern, not broad-based acute hospital growth. A single ME transplant-sized admission, NH back-problem admissions, and concentrated OH exposure at Euclid Hospital are driving most of the increase. Because only a small number of cases are responsible for a seven-figure change, case-level clinical and payment review is the right action.
business_patterns.why_it_matters: A handful of high-cost acute stays can distort market trends and often require different action than broad utilization growth.
business_patterns.recommended_next_step: Perform case-level clinical and reimbursement review for the ME, NH, and OH HMO acute admissions, focusing on transplant severity, back-problem inpatient necessity, and provider-specific pricing at Euclid Hospital.
business_patterns.validation_reason: The impact is concentrated in very few admissions with low-baseline and small-count flags, so confirmation is needed before broader policy action.
evidence_summary: A single ME HMO acute admission tied to liver transplant drove $486K.
NH IP Med/Surg back-problem cases under Medical Back Problems with MCC added $423K across 4 claims.
OH HMO acute spend at Euclid Hospital added $79K across 33 claims with higher paid per claim.

business_patterns.top_pattern: Orange County Global Medical Center is driving CA HMO acute hospital pressure
business_patterns.what_is_impacting: Commercial Individual HMO acute hospital spend in CA
key_driver_codes: Otitis Media and Upper Respiratory Infection without MCC
business_patterns.pattern_details: CA HMO acute hospital pressure is concentrated at Orange County Global Medical Center rather than spread across the market. Both volume and paid per admission increased, with one smaller DRG-specific unit-cost spike layered on top. This is best treated as a provider-specific economics and utilization issue.
business_patterns.why_it_matters: A concentrated provider pattern can often be addressed faster through targeted contract, payment, and UM action than through broad market changes.
business_patterns.recommended_next_step: Run a combined contract/payment accuracy review and acute admission UM audit for Orange County Global Medical Center, including outlier pricing and level-of-care checks.
business_patterns.validation_reason: The increase is concentrated in a low-volume provider run, so case and payment validation should precede broader network action.
evidence_summary: Orange County Global Medical Center added $589K on 19 additional HMO acute hospital claims, with about $31K higher paid per claim.
A separate CA HMO acute hospital unit-cost spike added $26K at flat volume in Otitis Media and Upper Respiratory Infection without MCC.

business_patterns.top_pattern: OH and UNATTRIBUTED show rare catastrophic IP Med/Surg cases
business_patterns.what_is_impacting: IP Med/Surg high-cost outlier admissions in OH and UNATTRIBUTED
key_driver_codes: Intracranial Hemorrhage or Cerebral Infarction with MCC
Septicemia or Severe Sepsis without Mechanical Ventilation >96 Hours with MCC
business_patterns.pattern_details: This segment is being driven by rare catastrophic inpatient Med/Surg cases, not by broad utilization expansion. The increase is concentrated in only three cases, led by a transplant-sized claim, with additional stroke and severe sepsis admissions. The right response is case-level clinical and payment validation rather than broad benefit or network changes.
business_patterns.why_it_matters: Catastrophic outliers can materially change trend results even when they are not repeatable patterns.
business_patterns.recommended_next_step: Open case-level clinical and payment validation for the transplant, stroke, and sepsis admissions to confirm severity, reimbursement accuracy, and any applicable outlier protections.
business_patterns.validation_reason: The spend is concentrated in a few very high-cost admissions and part of the segment is unattributed, so direct action requires claim-level confirmation.
evidence_summary: One liver transplant admission drove $486K.
A single stroke admission added $37K.
A single severe sepsis admission added $30K.

business_patterns.top_pattern: CA IP Med/Surg increase comes from a few new high-cost admissions
business_patterns.what_is_impacting: IP Med/Surg high-cost outlier admissions in CA
key_driver_codes: Other Major Cardiovascular Procedures with MCC
business_patterns.pattern_details: CA clinical pressure is coming from a very small number of expensive inpatient Med/Surg stays, led by one major cardiovascular procedure at Orange County Global Medical Center. Two smaller low-volume admissions add to the change, but the pattern is still case-specific rather than systemic. The action is focused clinical and reimbursement review of these outlier stays.
business_patterns.why_it_matters: A few severe inpatient cases can look like broad trend deterioration if they are not separated from routine utilization.
business_patterns.recommended_next_step: Review the CA outlier admissions for severity support, payment accuracy, and any reimbursement exceptions before pursuing wider clinical policy changes.
business_patterns.validation_reason: The increase is based on a handful of low-volume high-cost admissions, so case-level validation is required.
evidence_summary: One major cardiovascular procedure admission at Orange County Global Medical Center drove $427K.
Two additional low-volume IP Med/Surg admissions added about $73K combined.

business_patterns.top_pattern: IU Health Ball Memorial Hospital is a concentrated IN cost driver
business_patterns.what_is_impacting: Commercial Individual acute hospital, NICU, OB, and outpatient oncology spend in IN
key_driver_codes: Vaginal Delivery without Sterilization or D&C with CC
business_patterns.pattern_details: IN cost growth is concentrated at a single provider across both operational and clinical views. Acute HMO admissions are the largest piece, with additional isolated NICU, OB, and outpatient oncology episodes contributing smaller but still notable spend. This points to a provider-specific mix of reimbursement, authorization, and case-management issues rather than a broad statewide trend.
business_patterns.why_it_matters: When one provider drives multiple signals at once, coordinated action can address more spend than separate disconnected reviews.
business_patterns.recommended_next_step: Conduct a joint provider review for IU Health Ball Memorial Hospital covering acute HMO pricing, NICU and OB case management, and the small outpatient oncology outlier episode.
business_patterns.validation_reason: The pattern is heavily concentrated at one provider and much of the increase comes from low-volume outlier cases, so case-level confirmation is needed before broader action.
evidence_summary: IU Health Ball Memorial Hospital acute HMO admissions added $426K, including $293K tied directly to the provider.
One NICU prematurity case added $223K.
Smaller OB and outpatient oncology episodes added about $43K combined.

business_patterns.top_pattern: ME PPO spend is shifting into rehab and unattributed facility claims
business_patterns.what_is_impacting: Commercial Individual PPO non-acute facility spend in ME
business_patterns.pattern_details: ME PPO growth is occurring outside acute hospital settings, split between physical rehab and claims without usable facility mapping. Volume is the main driver in both areas, which suggests a possible site-of-care shift into post-acute or other non-acute settings. Because part of the pattern sits in Not Mapped facilities, mapping should be corrected before utilization policy is changed.
business_patterns.why_it_matters: Non-acute migration can create a durable spend shift if it is not distinguished from simple facility classification problems.
business_patterns.recommended_next_step: Validate ME PPO facility mapping first, then review physical rehab referral and authorization patterns to determine whether post-acute utilization controls need to be tightened.
business_patterns.validation_reason: Part of the increase is in Not Mapped facility claims, so the site-of-care story is not fully reliable until facility attribution is corrected.
evidence_summary: ME PPO Not Mapped facility claims added $158K on 60 more claims, with lower paid per claim.
ME PPO Physical Rehab added $134K on 48 more claims, with about $2.6K higher paid per claim.

executive_summary.headline: The overall story is a very large TX acute hospital utilization increase, with the rest of the change driven by concentrated provider-level outliers and material Not Mapped validation issues.
executive_summary.primary_business_message: TX HMO and POS acute hospital claims are the dominant cost driver and should be handled as a utilization and authorization problem first. Outside TX, the pattern shifts to provider concentration, rare high-cost inpatient cases, and a meaningful amount of spend sitting in Not Mapped buckets that must be fixed before downstream teams can act with confidence. The strongest business response is a split strategy: contain TX utilization, correct mapping, and work concentrated provider and case-level outliers in CA, ME/NH/OH, OH and UNATTRIBUTED, IN, and ME PPO non-acute settings.
recommended_focus_order: Contain TX acute hospital HMO and POS utilization growth.
Correct Not Mapped facility and clinical classification before broader policy or network action.
Work concentrated provider and rare high-cost case patterns in CA, ME/NH/OH, OH and UNATTRIBUTED, IN, and ME PPO non-acute settings.

notes: Validation issues were intentionally consolidated into one gating Not Mapped pattern across multiple segments.
The IN pattern intentionally combines operational and clinical groups because the signal is concentrated at the same provider and supports a single coordinated business action.
